items.title: Artigraph
items.text:
Artigraph is a Python library for building data products as versioned, fingerprinted artifacts — not just as task runs or loose files. You declare the artifacts your workflow should produce, connect them with producers, and Artigraph records the fingerprints and snapshot metadata needed to reproduce, inspect, and hand off a coherent version later.

Use Artigraph alongside the runner you already have. It is not a scheduler or orchestrator: scripts, cron, Airflow, Dagster, or another tool can decide when a workflow runs while Artigraph owns the data contract — types, storage, fingerprints, and snapshot lineage.

  • Try the playground

    The in-browser playground runs Artigraph in an isolated Pyodide filesystem so you can edit a small graph without installing Python locally.

    Open the playground

  • Run the local demo

    Start with Pandas, Parquet, SQLite metadata, and a snapshot-aware readback flow.

    uv run --all-extras --with duckdb python docs/examples/snapshot_parquet_duckdb/demo.py

items.title: What problem does this solve?
items.text:
After a pipeline has run a few times, "which files make up this dataset?" often becomes guesswork. A glob can pick up stale partitions; a rerun can overwrite an output you still needed; a downstream tool can silently mix versions.

Artigraph makes snapshot membership explicit. A version is something you can tag and reload, not a directory you hope is clean.

items.title: What Artigraph gives you
items.text:
• Artifacts describe the data product: type, format, storage, annotations, and statistics.
  • Producers describe how artifacts are built from other artifacts.
  • Fingerprints give artifacts, producers, partitions, and graph snapshots stable identities.
  • Snapshots let you tag and reload a coherent version of a graph later.
  • Storage metadata records which concrete partitions belong to a snapshot, so ecosystem tools can read the right files without guessing from path layout.

items.title: Recommended path
items.text:
1. Get started by building a small graph and running the tested local demos.
  2. Check status and fit for what works today and where Artigraph belongs in a stack.
  3. Read the graph lifecycle, then the core concepts: artifacts, producers, and snapshots/fingerprints.
  4. Run the snapshot-aware Pandas + Parquet example.
  5. Use the curated API reference for the public objects used in those examples.

items.title: Getting started
items.text: The fastest way to understand Artigraph is to build a small graph that writes real data, records fingerprints, and reads a snapshot back.

items.title: Install
items.text:
From a checkout:

uv sync --all-extras

From PyPI:

pip install arti

Add optional extras when you need them:

pip install 'arti[parquet]'  # Pandas/Parquet data files
pip install 'arti[sqlite]'   # durable local metadata

items.title: Build your first graph
items.text:
This example defines one raw artifact and one produced artifact, writes input data, builds a snapshot, and reads the result.

from typing import Annotated, TypedDict

from arti import Artifact, ArtifactStorage, Format, Graph, Type, producer
from arti.formats.json import JSON
from arti.storage.local import LocalFile
from arti.types import Collection, Float64, Int64, Struct
from arti.versions import SemVer


class Transactions(Artifact):
    type: Type = Collection(element=Struct(fields={"id": Int64(), "amount": Float64()}))
    format: Format = JSON()
    storage: ArtifactStorage = LocalFile(path="/tmp/artigraph-first-graph/transactions.json")


class TotalSpend(Artifact):
    type: Type = Float64()
    format: Format = JSON()
    storage: ArtifactStorage = LocalFile(
        path="/tmp/artigraph-first-graph/produced/{input_fingerprint}/total.json",
    )


class Transaction(TypedDict):
    id: int
    amount: float


@producer(version=SemVer(major=1, minor=0, patch=0))
def aggregate(
    transactions: Annotated[list[Transaction], Transactions],
) -> Annotated[float, TotalSpend]:
    return float(sum(transaction["amount"] for transaction in transactions))


with Graph(name="first-graph") as graph:
    graph.artifacts.transactions = Transactions()
    graph.artifacts.total = aggregate(transactions=graph.artifacts.transactions)


graph.write(
    [{"id": 1, "amount": 18.0}, {"id": 2, "amount": 24.0}],
    artifact=graph.artifacts.transactions,
)
snapshot = graph.build()
total = snapshot.read(snapshot.artifacts.total, annotation=float)
print(total)  # 42.0

The core steps are:

  • Artifact — the contract for a data product: type, format, and storage.
  • Producer — a versioned Python function that builds one artifact from another.
  • graph.write(...) — records raw input data before a build.
  • graph.build() — runs producers and returns a GraphSnapshot.
  • snapshot.read(...) — reads an artifact value from that exact snapshot.

See The graph lifecycle for tagging and reloading a snapshot later.

items.title: Run the small spend example
items.text:
The smallest tested example computes total spend from JSON transactions:

uv run python docs/examples/spend/demo.py

It finishes with:

INFO:root:Total Spend: 42.0

items.title: Run the local data-product demo
items.text:
The flagship local demo uses Pandas producers, partitioned Parquet outputs, durable SQLite metadata, and a snapshot-aware readback step:

uv run --all-extras --with duckdb python docs/examples/snapshot_parquet_duckdb/demo.py

Expected output includes:

Baseline snapshot total: 42.00
Corrected snapshot total: 39.50
Naive glob total: 51.50

DuckDB is just one ordinary tool that can consume the result. The user-facing benefit is that Artigraph supplies the exact files in a snapshot, so downstream tools do not guess from path globs or mix versions by accident.

items.title: Browser playground
items.text:
Run a real Artigraph graph in your browser. The Python runtime starts preparing in the background when the playground scrolls into view, so the first run may still take a moment. Later runs reuse the same initialized Pyodide worker and only reset the virtual filesystem before executing your code.

This is intentionally Artigraph-first: the sample defines artifacts, connects a producer, writes a raw partition, builds a snapshot, and reads the produced artifact back. There is no cloud account, external database, or DuckDB dependency in the playground path.

Run Stop Reset Loading... from datetime import date from pathlib import Path from typing import Annotated, TypedDict from arti import Artifact, ArtifactStorage, Format, Graph, PartitionKey, Type, producer from arti.formats.json import JSON from arti.partitions import DateField from arti.storage.local import LocalFile from arti.types import Collection, Date, Float64, Int64, Struct from arti.versions import SemVer class Transactions(Artifact): type: Type = Collection( element=Struct(fields={"id": Int64(), "date": Date(), "amount": Float64()}), partition_by=("date",), ) class TotalSpend(Artifact): type: Type = Float64() format: Format = JSON() storage: ArtifactStorage = LocalFile( path="/tmp/produced/{input_fingerprint}/total.json", ) class Transaction(TypedDict): id: int amount: float @producer(version=SemVer(major=1, minor=0, patch=0)) def aggregate_transactions( transactions: Annotated[list[Transaction], Transactions], ) -> Annotated[float, TotalSpend]: return float(sum(txn["amount"] for txn in transactions)) with Graph(name="browser-spend") as graph: graph.artifacts.transactions = Transactions( format=JSON(), storage=LocalFile(path="/tmp/transactions/{date.iso}.json"), ) graph.artifacts.total = aggregate_transactions(transactions=graph.artifacts.transactions) graph.write( [ {"id": 1, "date": "2026-01-01", "amount": 18.0}, {"id": 2, "date": "2026-01-01", "amount": 24.0}, ], artifact=graph.artifacts.transactions, partition_key=PartitionKey(date=DateField(value=date(2026, 1, 1))), ) snapshot = graph.build() total = snapshot.read(snapshot.artifacts.total, annotation=float) print(f"Snapshot id: {int(snapshot.id)}") print(f"Total spend: {total}") print("Produced files:") for path in sorted(Path("/tmp/produced").rglob("*.json")): print(f" {path}") result = {"total": total, "snapshot_id": int(snapshot.id)}

items.title: Browser sandbox
items.text: The playground runs in a Web Worker backed by Pyodide. It may download CodeMirror editor assets from esm.sh, Pyodide runtime files from the Pyodide CDN, and Artigraph wheels from this docs site, but it cannot access your local filesystem. Stopping a run, hitting the timeout, or reloading the page discards the worker.

items.title: Status and fit
items.text: Artigraph is an early-stage, pre-1.0 project hosted by the LF AI & Data Foundation as a Sandbox project. The core model — artifacts, producers, fingerprints, and snapshots — is ready to explore in local workflows, and the examples in these docs are tested. APIs in the curated reference are the public surface to start from; other modules may change faster. Use the project changelog to track changes between releases.

items.title: What works today
items.text:
• Python: 3.13 and 3.14, both tested in CI.
  • Storage: local files.
  • Formats: JSON and Parquet, with Parquet support focused on Pandas DataFrames.
  • Metadata backends: in-memory by default, SQLite for durable local metadata, and Postgres for a shared durable backend.
  • Core workflow: define artifacts and producers, write raw inputs, build a graph, tag a snapshot, and read a named snapshot back.
  • Ecosystem interop: hand exact snapshot files to outside tools, such as DuckDB, without relying on path globs.
  • Experimental: GCS storage (GCSFile), with JSON and pickle IO only.

items.title: Planned / not yet supported
items.text:
• Cloud Parquet IO.
  • Additional storage and format implementations.

The examples include short notes showing the intended shape of future cloud storage, but the tested path today is local-first.

items.title: Where Artigraph fits
items.text:
Artigraph is a library, not a scheduler. Use it with a script, cron, Airflow, Dagster, or any other runner when you want reproducible, versioned data artifacts with explicit snapshot lineage.

If you need task scheduling or a managed DAG, keep that tool. Let Artigraph own the data contract: types, storage, fingerprints, and the metadata that says which partitions belong to each snapshot.

items.title: Artifacts
items.text:
An artifact is Artigraph's contract for a data product. It says what the data represents, how it is serialized, where it lives, and what human or quality metadata is attached to it.

from arti import Artifact, ArtifactStorage, Format, Type
from arti.formats.json import JSON
from arti.storage.local import LocalFile
from arti.types import Float64


class TotalSpend(Artifact):
    type: Type = Float64()
    format: Format = JSON()
    storage: ArtifactStorage = LocalFile()

items.title: Artifact fields
items.text:
• type describes the logical shape of the data: scalar, struct, collection, partitions, and field types.
  • format describes how the data is serialized, such as JSON or Parquet.
  • storage describes where bytes are stored, such as a local file path template.
  • annotations attach domain metadata that should travel with the artifact definition.
  • statistics are intended for measured characteristics and quality signals.

items.title: Raw and produced artifacts
items.text:
Raw artifacts point at data that already exists or is written by the user. Produced artifacts are the outputs of producers. Produced artifact storage should include Artigraph's input fingerprint template, {input_fingerprint}, so that multiple versions can remain available at the same time:

LocalFile(path="/tmp/produced/{input_fingerprint}/total.json")

That version-preserving behavior is the foundation for reproducible snapshots: a corrected input can produce a new output without deleting the output that belonged to an older graph snapshot.

items.title: The graph lifecycle
items.text: The other concept pages describe Artigraph's nouns: artifacts, producers, snapshots, and fingerprints. This page describes the verbs that take a graph from definition to reproducible, reloadable data.

items.title: 1. Write raw inputs
items.text:
Raw artifacts hold data you supply. graph.write(...) serializes that data through the artifact's format and storage, then records a partition fingerprint.

graph.write(data, artifact=graph.artifacts.transactions)

Write raw inputs before building. graph.build() snapshots raw data and raises an error if a raw artifact has no data to snapshot.

items.title: 2. Build the graph
items.text:
graph.build() runs producers and returns a GraphSnapshot: a fingerprinted identity for this graph version, including the graph structure, artifact and producer definitions, raw partition fingerprints, and produced partition fingerprints.

snapshot = graph.build()

Artigraph does not decide when builds happen. You choose when to call build(); Artigraph records what data and definitions made that build reproducible. If an output partition with the same input fingerprint already exists, the local executor links it to the new snapshot instead of rebuilding it.

items.title: 3. Tag a snapshot
items.text:
A fingerprint is exact, but it is not memorable. Tag a snapshot when you want to name a version and load it later from a durable metadata backend.

snapshot.tag("baseline")

Tags are most useful with SQLite or Postgres metadata. With the default in-memory backend, tags only last as long as the Python process.

items.title: 4. Read or reload a coherent version
items.text:
Read an artifact from a snapshot you already have:

total = snapshot.read(snapshot.artifacts.total, annotation=float)

Or reload a tagged snapshot in a later process from a durable backend, then read from that exact version. This requires a graph built with that backend from importable definitions; see Metadata backends.

from arti import GraphSnapshot

snapshot = GraphSnapshot.from_tag("first-graph", "baseline", connectable=backend)
total = snapshot.read(snapshot.artifacts.total, annotation=float)

items.title: Why the order matters
items.text:
write → build → tag → read makes a version something you can name instead of a directory you hope is clean. Correcting an input and rebuilding produces a new snapshot without destroying the old one, so both versions can remain readable.

For the identity model behind this lifecycle, see Snapshots and fingerprints.

items.title: Metadata backends
items.text: A backend stores graph definitions, snapshots, tags, and storage partition metadata. The backend is metadata-only; artifact bytes still live in the configured storage system.

items.title: Memory
items.text: The default backend is in-process memory. It is useful for examples and tests, but it does not persist snapshots across processes.

items.title: SQLite
items.text:
SQLite is the recommended local durable backend:

from pathlib import Path

from arti.backends.sqlite import SQLiteBackend

backend = SQLiteBackend(path=Path("artigraph.sqlite"))

Use SQLite for local examples, notebooks, and demos where you want tags and snapshots to survive process restarts without running a service.

items.title: Postgres
items.text:
Postgres is intended for shared durable metadata:

from arti.backends.postgres import PostgresBackend

backend = PostgresBackend.from_url(
    "postgresql+psycopg://artigraph:password@localhost/artigraph",
)

Both SQL backends apply bundled Alembic migrations on first use by default. Set auto_upgrade=False if you want to control migrations explicitly.

items.title: Trust boundary
items.text: Persisted metadata includes module-qualified Python type paths, so artifact and producer definitions must live at module scope in an importable module. Definitions in a script run as __main__ cannot be persisted. Restoring graph metadata imports the recorded modules, so treat the backend as trusted infrastructure.

items.title: Producers
items.text:
A producer is a versioned Python transformation that builds one or more artifacts from input artifacts. This snippet uses the Transactions and TotalSpend artifacts from the first graph in Getting started.

from typing import Annotated

from arti import producer
from arti.versions import SemVer


@producer(version=SemVer(major=1, minor=0, patch=0))
def aggregate_transactions(
    transactions: Annotated[list[dict], Transactions],
) -> Annotated[float, TotalSpend]:
    return float(sum(txn["amount"] for txn in transactions))

items.title: How producers connect graphs
items.text:
Inside a Graph definition, calling a producer with artifact inputs creates a dependency edge. The producer is not just an ad-hoc task call: its code-facing signature, version, input artifacts, output artifacts, and partition mapping contribute to graph identity.

from arti import Graph

with Graph(name="spend") as graph:
    graph.artifacts.transactions = Transactions(...)
    graph.artifacts.total = aggregate_transactions(
        transactions=graph.artifacts.transactions,
    )

items.title: Partition mapping
items.text:
Partitioned producers decide which input partitions produce each output partition. The common case is one output partition for each input partition. This example mirrors the partitioned Parquet demo: raw is the producer parameter whose partitions drive the mapping, so each raw transaction partition produces one clean transaction partition.

from typing import Annotated

import pandas as pd

from arti import one_to_one, producer


@producer(map=one_to_one("raw"))
def clean_transactions(
    raw: Annotated[pd.DataFrame, RawTransactions],
) -> Annotated[pd.DataFrame, CleanTransactions]:
    return raw.copy()

Mapping is part of the data contract. It lets Artigraph record exactly which input partition fingerprints were used to build each output partition.

items.title: Snapshots and fingerprints
items.text: A fingerprint is Artigraph's stable identity primitive. Artifacts, producers, partition contents, and graph snapshots all use fingerprints so Artigraph can detect meaningful changes and preserve coherent versions.

items.title: What a graph snapshot means
items.text:
A GraphSnapshot identifies a graph at a point in time:

  • the graph structure,
  • artifact and producer definitions,
  • raw partition fingerprints,
  • produced partition fingerprints after a build,
  • and the storage partitions that belong to each artifact.

You can tag a snapshot and load it later from a durable backend:

snapshot = graph.build()
snapshot.tag("baseline")

same_snapshot = GraphSnapshot.from_tag(
    "spend",
    "baseline",
    connectable=backend,
)

items.title: Why fingerprints matter
items.text:
Fingerprints are not optional bookkeeping. They are the mechanism that lets Artigraph distinguish:

  • a new producer version from an old one,
  • a corrected partition from the partition it replaced,
  • a reused output partition from one that must be rebuilt,
  • and a coherent snapshot from a loose collection of files.

Artigraph currently uses FarmHash Fingerprint64 for string fingerprints and stores values as signed 64-bit integers for database and language interoperability.

items.title: Storage, formats, and views
items.text: Artigraph separates three concerns that are often tangled together in data workflows.

items.title: Storage
items.text:
Storage decides where bytes live. Local files, cloud objects, database tables, or future storage implementations can expose partitions through the same Artigraph storage model.

from arti.storage.local import LocalFile

storage = LocalFile(path="data/raw/{date.iso}.json")

Produced artifacts normally include {input_fingerprint} in their storage template so Artigraph can keep multiple output versions live at the same time.

items.title: Formats
items.text:
Formats decide how bytes are serialized. JSON is minimal and convenient. Parquet is a better fit for Pandas/DataFrame workflows and ecosystem tools.

from arti.formats.json import JSON
from arti.formats.parquet import Parquet

items.title: Views
items.text:
Views decide what Python object the caller reads or writes. A single logical artifact can be written as one view and read as another when adapters are registered.

The local Parquet example writes and reads Pandas DataFrame values while preserving Artigraph's artifact, partition, and snapshot metadata around those files.

items.title: Examples
items.text: Start with examples that produce and read real data locally. The examples are intentionally small, but they exercise Artigraph's central model: artifacts, producers, fingerprints, snapshots, and storage metadata.

items.title: Snapshot-aware Pandas + Parquet
items.text:
The flagship local example builds partitioned transaction data with Pandas, writes Parquet files, and uses Artigraph snapshot metadata to read a coherent version back.

Run the example

items.title: Spend
items.text:
The smaller spend example uses JSON files and Python values. It is useful when you want the fewest moving parts:

uv run python docs/examples/spend/demo.py

Or build and run it in Docker:

docker build --file docs/examples/spend/Dockerfile --tag artigraph/example-spend .
docker run --rm artigraph/example-spend

items.title: Ecosystem interop
items.text:
Artigraph-managed files are ordinary files. The difference is that Artigraph also records enough metadata for tools outside Artigraph to know which files belong to a snapshot.

Read about DuckDB interop

items.title: DuckDB ecosystem interop
items.text: DuckDB is useful when you want SQL over Artigraph-produced Parquet files. Any Parquet-aware tool can consume Artigraph outputs; DuckDB is a convenient example. The important part is that Artigraph tells the tool exactly which files belong to a snapshot.

items.title: The rule
items.text:
Use Artigraph metadata to choose files, then hand those files to DuckDB. This snippet uses the corrected snapshot and the snapshot_duckdb.py helper from the snapshot-aware Pandas + Parquet example.

import duckdb

from snapshot_duckdb import register_snapshot_view

with duckdb.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    register_snapshot_view(
        connection,
        snapshot=corrected,
        artifact=corrected.artifacts.clean,
        view_name="clean_transactions",
    )
    total = connection.sql(
        "SELECT sum(amount_usd) FROM clean_transactions",
    ).fetchone()[0]

You give DuckDB the files in a snapshot, not a folder to guess at. The helper resolves the Parquet files recorded for (GraphSnapshot, artifact_key), verifies that they still match their recorded fingerprints, and registers an in-memory DuckDB view over those exact files. You can copy this helper into your own project; it is not part of Artigraph's public API yet.

items.title: Why not just use storage paths?
items.text: In simple storage layouts a glob might appear to work, but a glob is still a convention rather than a snapshot. Artigraph's storage model allows multiple produced versions to remain live at once. That is useful for reproducibility and cache reuse. When you want a coherent graph version, the source of truth is the snapshot metadata.

items.title: Snapshot-aware Pandas + Parquet
items.text: This local demo shows the core Artigraph workflow. A graph defines raw and cleaned transaction artifacts, a Pandas producer writes partitioned Parquet outputs, Artigraph records fingerprints for each produced partition, and named graph snapshots let you read back a coherent version later. The DuckDB query at the end shows the payoff: an outside tool gets the correct answer because it reads exactly the files in the snapshot, not whatever a glob happens to match.

items.title: Run it
items.text:
From the repository root:

uv run --all-extras --with duckdb python docs/examples/snapshot_parquet_duckdb/demo.py

The command uses only local files, an in-memory DuckDB connection, and a local SQLite metadata database under _work/. It does not require Docker, cloud credentials, or an external service.

Expected output includes:

Naive glob files: 3 for 2 logical snapshot partitions
Shared files across snapshots: 1
Baseline-only files: 1
Corrected-only files: 1
Baseline snapshot files: 2
Corrected snapshot files: 2
Baseline snapshot total: 42.00
Corrected snapshot total: 39.50
Naive glob total: 51.50 (wrong: it mixes live versions from both snapshots)

The generated file list also exposes the input fingerprint in every produced path. One unchanged day is reused, while the corrected day has old and new Parquet files under different fingerprint directories. The naive glob reads three physical files for two logical partitions, mixing versions from different snapshots and returning a wrong total. Snapshot metadata avoids exactly this.

items.title: Snapshot-aware ecosystem access
items.text:
The cleaned artifact's storage template includes {input_fingerprint}. Correcting a raw daily partition creates a new cleaned partition without deleting the old version. You get this for free: past snapshots stay reproducible, while the corrected snapshot points at the new output.

When another tool wants to read those files, it should start from Artigraph's snapshot metadata instead of reconstructing membership from storage layout conventions. The helper in snapshot_duckdb.py looks up the partitions linked to (GraphSnapshot, artifact_key). Before passing those exact paths to DuckDB, it checks that every partition is local Parquet, exists, and still matches its recorded content fingerprint. DuckDB stays in memory and never creates a database file.

The interop pattern is: register a DuckDB view from a specific Artigraph snapshot, then query that view like any other DuckDB relation.

import duckdb

from snapshot_duckdb import register_snapshot_view

with duckdb.connect(":memory:") as connection:
    register_snapshot_view(
        connection,
        snapshot=corrected,
        artifact=corrected.artifacts.clean,
        view_name="clean_transactions",
    )
    total = connection.sql("SELECT sum(amount_usd) FROM clean_transactions").fetchone()[0]

items.title: Limitation: raw local inputs
items.text: Overwriting a raw local path does not preserve the old raw bytes. Artigraph records their fingerprints, but local storage is not automatically content-addressed. Cross-snapshot interop queries in this demo therefore target produced artifacts, whose input-fingerprint paths preserve both versions.

items.title: Extending this to GCS later
items.text:
The artifact format and Pandas producer code can remain the same; the storage implementation is the main swap:

# Local demo
from arti.storage.local import LocalFile

storage = LocalFile.rooted_at(work_dir / "data" / "produced")

# Possible future GCS variant
from arti.storage.google.cloud.storage import GCSFile

storage = GCSFile(
    bucket="my-artigraph-demo-bucket",
    path="demo/{graph_name}/{names}/{partition_key_spec}/{input_fingerprint}/{name}{extension}",
)

The GCS snippet shows a possible future extension shape. It is not a tested path today and this example does not provision cloud resources.

items.title: Reference
items.text:
This reference is intentionally curated. It documents the public objects used by the getting-started path and examples, not every internal module.

  • Core API: graph construction, artifacts, producers, snapshots, fingerprints, and IO helpers.

If an object is not included here, treat it as less stable unless the source code or release notes say otherwise.

items.title: Core API
items.text: The examples import these objects from arti when they are re-exported there. The reference entries use canonical module paths so the generated docs can resolve them reliably.

items.title: arti.graphs.Graph
items.text:
Bases: Model

Graph stores a web of Artifacts connected by Producers.

items.title: snapshot(*, connection=None)
items.text:
Identify a "unique" ID for this Graph at this point in time.

The ID aims to encode the structure of the Graph plus a snapshot of the raw Artifact data (partition kinds and contents). Any change that would affect data should prompt an ID change, however changes to this ID don't directly cause data to be reproduced.

NOTE: There is currently a gap (and thus race condition) between when the Graph ID is computed and when we read raw Artifacts data during Producer builds.

items.title: arti.artifacts.Artifact
items.text:
Bases: Model

An Artifact is the base structure describing an existing or generated dataset.

An Artifact is comprised of three key elements: - type: spec of the data's structure, such as data types, nullable, etc. - format: the data's serialized format, such as CSV, Parquet, database native, etc. - storage: the data's persistent storage system, such as blob storage, database native, etc.

In addition to the core elements, an Artifact can be tagged with additional annotations (to associate it with human knowledge) and statistics (to track derived characteristics over time).

items.title: cast(value) classmethod
items.text:
Attempt to convert an arbitrary value to an appropriate Artifact instance.

Artifact.cast is used to convert values assigned to an ArtifactBox (such as Graph.artifacts) into an Artifact. When called with: - an Artifact instance, it is returned - a Producer instance with a single output Artifact, the output Artifact is returned - a Producer instance with a multiple output Artifacts, an error is raised - other types, we attempt to map to a Type and return an Artifact instance with defaulted Format and Storage

items.title: arti.fingerprints.Fingerprint
items.text:
Bases: int64

Fingerprint represents a unique identity as an int64 value.

Using an int(64) has a number of convenient properties: - can be combined independent of order with XOR - can be stored relatively cheaply - 0 acts as an "identity" value when combined (5 ^ 0 = 5) - is relatively cross-platform (across databases, languages, etc)
